questions.q: What do model risk management frameworks like SR 11-7 actually mandate?
options: A specific software vendor that every bank must use
Capabilities: independent validation before deployment, ongoing monitoring, documented limitations, and a record of who approved what and when
That models can never be updated after initial deployment
A minimum model accuracy of 99%
questions.explain: SR 11-7 specifies required capabilities rather than mandating particular tools — platform tooling like registries and approval gates is how teams satisfy those capabilities.

questions.q: Why does the example model card include `auc_by_region` instead of only one overall AUC number?
options: Regional breakdowns are required by GDPR specifically
Aggregate performance can hide that a model performs worse in a specific segment, so slice-level results are what a real review actually checks
It makes the model train faster
Region is a required field in all JSON files
questions.explain: A model card that reports only one aggregate metric and omits where the model underperforms doesn't give a reviewer what they need to assess risk properly.

questions.q: Why must an audit log be "immutable" (write-once)?
options: Immutability makes the log load faster for dashboards
A log that can be edited or deleted after an incident defeats the entire purpose of having an audit trail
It is a formatting requirement with no functional purpose
Mutable logs are not supported by any database
questions.explain: If entries could be altered after the fact, the log could no longer be trusted as evidence of what actually happened, undermining its purpose.

questions.q: To answer "show me everything about the model that made decision X," what three pieces does the lesson say need to connect?
options: Only the model's source code
The audit log (which version was active at that time), the model card/manifest (what it was trained on and how evaluated), and the approval record (who signed off)
Only the final deployed container image
A single spreadsheet maintained manually by the compliance team
questions.explain: None of the three pieces alone answers a full audit request — together, connected by model version and timestamp, they do.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say "we have the data somewhere" is not the same as being auditable?
options: Because regulators only accept physical paper records
Because auditability requires the chain to be retrievable on demand, in a reasonable timeframe, by a defined process — not merely reconstructible if someone searches long enough
Because data cannot legally be stored electronically
Because having data anywhere automatically satisfies any audit
questions.explain: A team that technically has the data but takes weeks to assemble it for an auditor has functionally failed the audit — retrievability on demand is the actual bar.
